final_proof:
Let \((X,\Sigma)\) be a measurable space; thus \(\Sigma\subseteq\mathcal P(X)\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(X\). We show that ordinary union makes \(\Sigma\) a magma of sets. Recall that a magma is a nonempty set equipped with a binary operation, and a magma of sets is one whose elements are sets and whose operation is a set operation.

First, \(\Sigma\) is nonempty, since the \(\sigma\)-algebra axioms give \(X\in\Sigma\). Let \(A,B\in\Sigma\). Define a sequence \((E_n)_{n\geq 1}\) of members of \(\Sigma\) by
\[
E_1=A,\qquad E_n=B\quad(n\geq 2).
\]
Because \(\Sigma\) is closed under countable unions,
\[
\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}E_n\in\Sigma.
\]
But this union is exactly \(A\cup B\). Hence \(A\cup B\in\Sigma\) whenever \(A,B\in\Sigma\). It follows that the restriction of ordinary union is a well-defined map
\[
\cup:\Sigma\times\Sigma\longrightarrow\Sigma.
\]
Therefore \((\Sigma,\cup)\) is a magma. Since every element of \(\Sigma\) is a subset of \(X\) and its multiplication is the usual set union, it is a magma of sets. Thus every \(\sigma\)-algebra is an instance of a magma of sets. \(\square\)
